paragraphs: Exploration checklist | This occupation, 43-9061.00, handles varied general clerical duties. O*NET core tasks include equipment, telephones, communication, filing, retrieving information, mail, and proofreading. Money handling, accounting, and documents are supplemental tasks. Among respondents, 15% work more than 40 hours weekly, 59% work 40 hours, and 26% fewer than 40 hours. Questionnaires are not proof of hiring suitability or competence; first check target work objects, systems, and authority.

Experience suggestion | Use the complete six fictional G1 materials in the pathway section. In 60 minutes, create a four-item transaction ledger, B01 amount and approval check, and three-area filing handover. Recalculate 100 yuan, 8.70%, 18 / 50 minutes, and the 30-minute meeting. Compare with reference answers. Make no payments, external disclosures, actual messages, or file deletions; no external template or expert is needed.

Fit signals | U.S. O*NET 43-9061.00 work-activity importance identifies the main activities as working with computers, 81; communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates, 76; getting information, 72; performing administrative activities, 68; documenting and recording information, 64; establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships, 63; processing information, 63; and communicating with people outside the organization, 62. Work context shows importance of being exact or accurate, 77% extremely important; constant contact with others, 82%; telephone, 93% daily; email, 89% daily; environmentally controlled indoor work, 90% daily; sitting, 60% continually or almost continually; repeating the same tasks, 66% extremely important; external customers or the public, 65% extremely important; decision-making freedom, 34% some freedom; determining tasks, priorities, and goals, 40% limited freedom; and impact on coworkers' or company results, 45% very important results. If you enjoy handling varied tasks under processes and rules, remain careful and accurate amid multitasking and deadlines, communicate frequently with people and organizations, and record truthfully, this occupation's daily demands are closer to your working style.

Caution signals | Repeated checks, multitasking, and frequent communication require patience. Roles involving funds, personal information, or contracts also require checks of rules and authority. The U.S. projection of −6% describes national job totals only, not individual employment or outsourcing and GenAI effects. Use G1 to check whether urgency still leads you to skip checks and documentation.

Judging the responsibility | Real fit depends on doing three things within one administrative task: complete the work properly, using office systems and procedures for receipt, registration, classification, entry, filing, replies, and referral while ensuring accurate information, amounts, periods, and parties; maintain compliance and verifiability, handling payments, contracts, and documents under authority, limits, and approvals, processing personal information and business data by minimum necessity, and documenting all steps for review; and accept defined role responsibilities, being accountable for your entry, filing, replies, and referral and reporting or handing over matters beyond authority or procedures. Test this through a verifiable exercise, such as a transaction ledger and handover note for fictional materials, a payment and document-checking procedure, an archive and retention-period list, or a review of a data-leak or unauthorized-request response drill, rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

Work categories | Telephones and communication, equipment and word processing, records and retrieval, data checking, scheduling, and supplies support. Money handling, basic bookkeeping, and documents are O*NET supplemental tasks, not duties of every role. The editorial process is receipt and registration—classification and checking—processing within authority—records and handover. Check specific duties and authority against organizational rules first.

Occupational profile | 43-9061.00 General Office Clerks perform varied general clerical duties. O*NET2026 is updated and labeled Bright Outlook. Core tasks include equipment, 89; telephones, 84; communication, 82; updating filing, inventory, and databases, 76; organizing and filing, 75; retrieving information and mail, 73 each; proofreading, 69; scheduling, 68; word processing, 64; supplies, 63; and conveying messages, 62. Money handling and basic bookkeeping, 79; completing and mailing documents, 78; and business forms, 71, are supplemental, not universal duties. Importance uses a 0—100 score, not time shares. Activities include computers, 81; coworker communication, 76; getting information, 72; administrative activities, 68; and records, 64.

entries: Receipt and communication | Calls and visitors | Answer and route calls, take messages, and communicate with customers, employees, and others to answer questions, convey or explain information, receive orders, handle complaints, and communicate outside the organization.

Office equipment and software | Tools and systems | Operate copiers, scanners, fax machines, voicemail systems, and personal computers and use office, spreadsheet, and accounting software for entry, formatting, statistics, and queries.

Records and information management | Filing and retrieval | Maintain and update filing, inventory, mailing, and database systems; compile, copy, sort, and file office-activity and business-transaction records; and retrieve files and records to respond to requests.

Documents and bookkeeping | Receipts, payments, and vouchers | Supplemental tasks, subject to the specific role: collect, count, and pay money, perform basic bookkeeping and banking transactions, complete and mail bills, contracts, policies, invoices, or checks, and process business or government forms and expense claims.

Data checking and entry | Accuracy and documentation | Calculate, record, and proofread data and other information such as records or reports, ensuring accurate amounts, periods, parties, and identifiers, with system records and procedural review.

Coordination and support | Schedules and supplies | Arrange meetings, schedules, travel, and office supplies and work with superiors and colleagues on cross-department tasks, handover, filing, and ad hoc requests.

Communication | Telephone, 93% daily; email, 89% daily; constant contact with others, 82%; face-to-face individual or team discussions, 74% daily; letters and memos, 33% daily; communicating outside the organization, work-activity importance 62.
Setting and environment | Environmentally controlled indoors, 90% daily; somewhat close physical proximity, such as shared offices, 45%; using hands to handle, control, or feel objects and tools, 39% never.
Accuracy and consequences | Being exact or accurate, 77% extremely important; impact on coworkers' or company results, 45% very important results; consequences of errors not easily corrected: 13% extremely serious, 14% very serious, 37% fairly serious. These response distributions are not accident rates.
Teams and collaboration | Working in or contributing to a team, 64% extremely important; coordinating or leading others, 34% important; external customers or the public, 65% extremely important.
Decisions and autonomy | Decision-making freedom, 34% some freedom; determining tasks, priorities, and goals, 40% limited freedom; decision frequency, 33% daily.
Repetition and pace | Repeating the same tasks, 66% extremely important; repetitive motions, 33% continually or almost continually; time pressure, 42% weekly or more but not daily, with another 24% daily; sitting, 60% continually or almost continually.
Communication difficulties | Unpleasant, angry, or discourteous people, 44% yearly or more but not monthly, with another 20% daily; external customers or the public, 65% extremely important.
Hours and workload | Typical workweek: 15% more than 40 hours, 59% at 40 hours, and 26% fewer than 40 hours. Paper, documents, calls, and visitors create multitasking and deadline pressure.
Compliance and boundaries | Personal information and business data follow minimum necessity, permissions, and retention. Payments, contracts, seals, and external commitments require authorized-person or organizational-process approval; clerks do not substitute for approvers.

Task and record guidance | Begin with receipt and registration. Under office procedures, check the source, matter, amount, period, and deadline of documents, calls, mail, and vouchers, classify and prioritize, confirm authority, limits, and approval requirements, then process, enter, file, reply, or refer. Payments, contracts, document signatures, seals, and external commitments require authority. Limit purposes and permissions for personal information, business data, and customer materials. Important judgments, communications, documentation, and handovers must be reviewable by superiors and checking roles in ledgers and systems.

Receipt and registration → classification and priorities → authority and limit checks → processing, entry, and filing → replies, referral, and documentation → review, handover, and anomaly reporting

Information and records | Customer and employee data about identified or identifiable natural persons fall under the Personal Information Protection Law. Check financial accounts, health, and other sensitive personal information separately under Article 28; not all business transactions are sensitive personal information. Check lawful bases, necessary scope, permissions, sharing, and retention. Truthfully supplement and traceably correct ordinary transaction ledgers without fabrication or backdating. Original accounting vouchers must not be altered; the issuer must reissue those with amount errors, and other errors follow Article 14. Correct accounting books under Article 15. Dispose of archives after appraisal, approval, and applicable rules; do not universally prohibit lawful destruction.

Records and collaboration | Under organizational office and archive-management rules, record receipt, classification, checking, processing, entry, filing, replies, referral, and review using required templates and deadlines. Immediately pause mismatched amounts, periods, or parties, missing approvals or limits, abnormal vouchers, unauthorized personal-information access, or requests exceeding authority, then report and seek review within authority. Do not alter ledgers without a trace. Truthful supplementary entries and corrections identify people and times and preserve originals.

Adjacent boundaries | This occupation handles varied general clerical work. 43-6011 covers executive secretaries and executive administrative assistants; 43-6014 covers secretaries and administrative assistants other than legal, medical, and executive roles, so both cannot be called executive support. Document management specialists 15-1299.03 emphasize enterprise electronic-document systems and management procedures; 43-9071 covers office machine operators. Reception 43-4171, bookkeeping 43-3031, entry 43-9021, and supervision 43-1011 are classified by primary tasks, which may overlap. Classification grants no contract or payment authority.

Core principles of adjacent roles | Most roles in the same group and adjacent roles aim to process tasks accurately under procedures and rules and leave reliable, retrievable information and service records. They differ in task breadth, authority level, and contacts: general clerical task combinations, support for specific managers, reception and information guidance, bookkeeping records, bulk data entry, archive lifecycles, or team and process management.

This occupation's core purpose | Handle daily office tasks within authority, processes, and rules through receipt, registration, classification, processing, entry, filing, replies, and referral: calls and routing, equipment and software, records and information management, documents and bookkeeping, data checking and entry, and coordination and support. Make accuracy and traceability reviewable and meet compliance and information-protection requirements.

Main objects and basis of adjacent roles | Administrative assistants and executive secretaries follow specific managers' scheduling, correspondence, meeting, travel, and confidentiality requirements; receptionists and information clerks follow visitor reception, guidance, and telephone standards; bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks follow accounting, voucher, reconciliation, and report-support requirements; data entry keyers follow bulk-entry, validation, and accuracy requirements; document-management specialists follow classification, retention, compliance, and retrieval requirements; first-line office-support supervisors follow scheduling, process, quality, personnel, and budget-management requirements.

Main objects and basis of this occupation | Address daily office tasks, including calls, visitors, mail, incoming documents, vouchers, forms, files, supplies, and schedules, and office systems such as office software, spreadsheets, accounting, databases, filing, and scanning. The basis is office procedures, authority and limit rules, finance, voucher and money-handling requirements, personal-information, data-security and archive-management requirements, and customer-service and confidentiality requirements.

General office clerks handle varied general clerical work, requiring familiarity with office systems and procedures. Tasks may involve telephones, word processing, equipment, and filing; the organization defines the mix. Money handling and basic bookkeeping are supplemental, not universal duties.

Core processes of adjacent roles | Administrative assistants and executive secretaries focus on managers' schedules, correspondence, meetings, travel, and information filtering; receptionists and information clerks on reception, visitor guidance, and call routing; bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks on voucher entry, reconciliation, aging, and report preparation; data entry keyers on bulk entry and format validation; document-management specialists on classification, cataloging, borrowing, destruction, and compliant retention; office-support supervisors on scheduling, processes, quality metrics, personnel, and outsourcing.

Core process of this occupation | Receive and register, checking sources, matters, and deadlines; classify and prioritize, confirming authority and limits; process, enter, and proofread amounts and periods; file, reply, refer, and document within scope; review, hand over, and update ledgers; and pause and report anomalies, exceeded authority, or suspected risks. Document each step under office, finance, and archive rules for superior and checking-role inspection.

Main outputs of adjacent roles | Administrative assistants and executive secretaries produce manager schedules, correspondence, minutes, travel, and information-submission records; receptionists and information clerks produce reception, visitor, call, routing, and guidance records; bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks produce vouchers, books, reconciliations, and report-support records; data entry keyers produce structured-entry and validation records; document-management specialists produce archive catalogs, borrowing, destruction, and retention records; office-support supervisors produce scheduling, process, quality, and personnel-management records.

Main outputs of this occupation | Verifiable transaction ledgers and handover notes with receipt times, sources, matters, processing steps, handlers, and reviewers; call, visitor, mail, and incoming-document registration, replies, and referral records; document, money-handling, basic-bookkeeping, limit, and approval checks; data-entry and proofreading records; filing, retrieval, borrowing, and retention-period records; and office-supply, schedule, and meeting records.

Responsibility in adjacent roles | Responsibilities in the same group and adjacent roles are usually defined by the organization, role authority, and procedures and generally concern organizations, customers, coworkers, business data, and fund security.

Responsibility in this occupation | Be accountable for personally handled receipt, classification, entry, proofreading, filing, replies, referral, and ledgers and for procedural authorized checking and review. Appropriately authorized roles or organizations decide under rules on payments, contracts, seals, external commitments, accounting, tax and audit judgments, external personal-information and business-data provision, archive destruction, major fund errors, and information leaks. This occupation does not replace their decisions.

Authority and approval in adjacent roles | Authority comes from role delegation, processes, and rules and generally excludes independent payment, contract, external-commitment, or accounting decisions beyond personal authority. Refer fund, contract, personal-information, and archive-disposal matters to appropriately authorized roles or organizations.

Authority and approval in this occupation | Receipt, registration, entry, proofreading, filing, replies, and referral must remain within role authority, processes, and limits. Payments, reimbursements, contracts, seals, external commitments, external or cross-border personal-information and business-data provision, archive destruction, and fund or voucher handling beyond limits or designated persons require approval or referral under rules. Do not sign for others or process beyond authority.

Limits on conclusions in adjacent roles | Conclusions generally remain at role, process, and organizational level and usually do not establish financial authenticity, contract validity, legal opinions, or accounting assurance. Cross-department conclusions and those involving funds, contracts, or assurance have scope limits.

Limits on conclusions in this occupation | State only verifiable receipt, processing, entry, and filing facts, distinguishing closed matters, missing materials, and authorized-processing needs. Do not make unauthorized judgments or commitments beyond authority or processes, such as payment approval, contract-signature validity, accounting assurance, or legal opinions. Pause and escalate or refer mismatched amounts or periods, missing approvals or limits, suspected fabricated vouchers, personal-information leakage risks, and unauthorized requests. Descriptions must withstand superior, review, internal-control, audit, and regulatory inspection.

Checks before joining | Use the following six items one by one before applying or joining to avoid inferring duties and authority from titles or promotional wording. Base findings on written recruitment information, employment contracts, job descriptions, authorization, and rule documents and continue confirming after joining. This page lists checking directions only, not any organization's formal requirements. Special note: this occupation often involves money handling, personal information, contracts, and archives. Confirm authority, limits, review, seals, information access, and confidentiality requirements.

Checking guidance | Similar titles can have very different duties and authority. Some emphasize reception, telephones, and front-desk service; others entry and documents, bookkeeping and voucher support, archives and records, or general task support. Money-handling powers, seals and contract processes, information access and confidentiality, duty coverage, and overtime arrangements vary by organization.

01 Actual duties and authority boundaries | Check whether the role independently receives, processes, enters, files, and replies or supports work under guidance. Check permitted money handling, limits, approval and review, seals, contracts and external correspondence processes, personal-information and business-data access and sharing permissions and confidentiality, and ownership and escalation paths for cross-department tasks.

Checking suggestion | Ask about sitting and screen-work arrangements, breaks, complaints, and anti-harassment channels. For specific confidential or fund-handling roles, check the basis, scope, and training for background checks. This page has no evidence that all clerks generally need health examinations or background verification.

02 Information, funds, confidentiality, and compliance | Check whether the organization requires and provides fund, voucher, reimbursement, limit, approval, and review rules and training; authority and processes for seals, contracts, external correspondence, and commitments; personal-information and business-data access, minimum necessity, retention, and confidentiality training; archive and record filing, borrowing, and destruction standards; training on fraud, conflicts of interest, complaints, whistleblowing, and information-security incident reporting and response; and corresponding background checks and confidentiality agreements.

Checking guidance | U.S. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 1—2, little to some preparation, with an SVP range below 6.0 and usually a high-school diploma or equivalent. The O*NET education survey shows 41% requiring high-school or equivalent education, 36% an associate or other two-year degree, and 15% some college. BLS's education and training crosswalk lists typical high-school or equivalent entry education, no related experience, and short-term on-the-job training. This does not replace employer and competent-authority credential and training requirements.

03 Education, training, and skills | Check requirements for high-school or equivalent education, vocational education, or an associate degree; specific office, spreadsheet, accounting, database, or industry-system skills, such as healthcare or education administration, and typing speed; industry experience such as healthcare, education, government, or construction; continuing training and skill updates; and internal authority conditions for independently handling funds, archives, and information systems.

Checking suggestion | O*NET respondents report 15% above 40 hours weekly, 59% at 40 hours, and 26% below 40 hours; this does not establish widespread overtime. Ask the target employer about peak periods, overtime, duty arrangements, and contractual wage components.

04 Pay, hours, and contract definitions | Check compensation components: base pay, performance or attendance pay, overtime and subsidies, and skill or role allowances. Check hours, overtime, duty coverage, peak periods, probation and assessment definitions, and internal responsibility, confidentiality, and noncompete arrangements concerning fund errors, information leaks, and third-party losses.

Checking guidance | Interfaces with superiors, colleagues, finance, human resources, external customers, and suppliers define responsibility boundaries for tasks, funds, information, and filing and must be clarified beforehand.

05 Authority at interfaces with finance, human resources, business, and outsourcing roles | Check submission, approval, and review interfaces for funds, vouchers, and reimbursement; application and authorization paths for seals, contracts, and external correspondence; personal-information and business-data access, sharing, and external-provision approval; archive and record filing, borrowing, and destruction interfaces; and reporting and handover arrangements for anomalies, complaints, and information-security incidents.

Checking guidance | Traceability and documentation requirements for ledgers, vouchers, archives, replies, and handovers define task, fund, information, and responsibility boundaries. Clarify templates, deadlines, amendments, archiving, permissions, and retention beforehand; personal information and business data also follow minimum necessity and permission rules.

06 Ledgers, vouchers, archives, and documentation | Check transaction ledgers and handover notes; call, visitor, mail, and incoming-document registration, replies, and referrals; money handling, reimbursement, limit approval, review, and two-person checks; data-entry and proofreading records; filing, retrieval, borrowing, retention, and destruction records; and templates, deadlines, amendments, archiving, retention, and access rules. Check evidence and cooperation duties during internal-control, audit, regulatory, and complaint reviews, and requirements for truthful records, truthful supplementary entries, authorized traceable corrections, and compliant retention and disposal.

This table makes no numerical comparisons or wage proxies across occupations. Check authority and compliance boundaries against each jurisdiction and organizational rules.

Introduction | The comparison has four columns: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which choices it better suits. General clerical work, administrative assistance, reception, bookkeeping support, data entry, and archive management often connect within one organization, but connection does not mean interchangeability. Changing direction requires learning role authority, professional definitions, compliance, and responsibility boundaries.

Comparison note | Occupations differ by primary tasks and outputs, with possible overlap. General clerks handle varied tasks; other directions focus more on reception, bookkeeping, entry, secretarial support, or enterprise document systems. Classification does not determine authority levels or exclude specific role responsibilities.

Exploration suggestion | If willing to switch among varied tasks, calls, mail, and vouchers while maintaining accuracy and documentation, try G1. Accuracy does not guarantee a stable or predictable pace.

Tasks and outputs | Telephones, equipment, word processing, and records are general tasks; ledgers, replies, and filing are reviewable. Money handling, basic bookkeeping, and documents are supplemental tasks determined by role and authority.
This occupation: General Office Clerks (43-9061.00)

Difference | Executive secretaries and executive administrative assistants 43-6011 emphasize senior-executive support. 43-6014 covers secretaries and administrative assistants other than legal, medical, and executive roles, supporting everyday office business rather than all serving executives. General clerks are classified by a varied general-task mix; duties may overlap. Organizational delegation determines authority.

Exploration suggestion | Compare secretarial directions if you prefer schedules, meetings, and correspondence. First check actual support recipients, confidentiality, and authority; titles cannot establish contact levels.

Core work and outputs: arrange and maintain managers' schedules, meetings, and travel; draft and organize correspondence, reports, and minutes; filter and forward information and incoming items; and coordinate internal and external communication and reception. Outputs are manager schedules, correspondence, minutes, travel, and information-submission records.
Administrative Assistants and Executive Secretaries (Secretaries and Administrative Assistants / Executive Secretaries, 43-6011 / 43-6014 and related codes)

Key difference: receptionists and information clerks focus on front-door and front-desk reception, visitor guidance, call routing, and information, emphasizing first contact with external visitors and calls. This occupation is broader, covering records, documents, data, and filing, with reception only one part.
Better suited to people who want first contact with visitors and callers and emphasize service presentation and immediate response; this occupation emphasizes back-office tasks and records.

Core work and outputs: receive, verify, register, and guide visitors; answer and route calls and provide or retrieve information; receive and refer requests, appointments, parcels, and letters; and maintain reception, visitor, and call records. Outputs are reception, visitor, call, routing, and information-guidance records.
Receptionists and Information Clerks (43-4171)

Difference | 43-3031 focuses more on financial records, vouchers, and reconciliation. General clerks may perform supplemental basic bookkeeping depending on the role. Classification grants no audit-assurance or payment-approval authority and cannot prove they never support reports.

Better suited to people who want voucher, reconciliation, and report-support work under accounting and finance definitions and accept stricter amount and period accuracy; this occupation emphasizes general tasks and documents.

Core work and outputs: enter and review original vouchers and post books; reconcile banks, counterparties, and expenses and handle discrepancies; organize aging, receivables, payables, and report-support data; and supply vouchers and explanations for month-end close and audits. Outputs are vouchers, books, reconciliations, and report-support records.
Bookkeeping, Accounting, and Auditing Clerks (43-3031)

Key difference: data entry keyers focus on high-volume structured entry, format validation, and accuracy, with highly focused repetitive tasks. This occupation's tasks are more dispersed and include communication, documents, filing, and coordination, with less repetition within one task.
Better suited to people who can sustain intensive repetitive entry with high accuracy; this occupation emphasizes varied task combinations and communication.

Core work and outputs: enter paper or source data into systems under rules and templates, validate formats, ranges, and required fields, handle returns and corrections, and track progress and accuracy. Outputs are structured-entry, validation, and progress records.
Data Entry Keyers (43-9021)

Difference | Document management specialists 15-1299.03 manage enterprise electronic-document systems and procedures, including classification, retrieval, access and sharing controls, retention, and disposal. General clerks may perform everyday filing, with overlapping duties. 43-9071 covers office machine operators, not document management specialists.
Better suited to people who want to manage record lifecycles, retrieval, and retention under archive and compliance definitions; this occupation emphasizes daily tasks and immediate filing.

Outputs | Enterprise electronic-document systems, classification schemes, access and retrieval processes, and document-management standards, with IT collaboration on implementation. Check whether paper archives and destruction approval are included in the specific role.

values: G1 is entirely fictional, received on October 1, 2026 at 09:00. Use only paper or offline spreadsheets and a calculator, without real systems, payments, or contact with real people.

Incoming R1: at 09:00, reimbursement application B01 shows 1,250 yuan, while the invoice shows 1,150 yuan, period September 2026, party S01, approval blank. R2: at 09:05, asks whether B01 can be paid that day, with a reply deadline of 10:00.

Incoming R3: at 09:06, requests a financial-account list for employee identifiers E01/E02 in a public group, due 09:30. Incoming R4: at 09:07, meeting M01 is approved by meeting lead Q for October 2, 2026, 10:00—10:30, indoor meeting room A, with notice due by 11:00.

Exercise authority: the clerk may only register, check, refer, and draft replies, with no payment or approval powers and no public disclosure of financial accounts. Finance F handles reimbursement, information lead I handles R3, and Q handles meetings. Referred to F at 09:10 and I at 09:12; neither has replied.

Exercise archive rules: B01 and vouchers go in the finance area; record linked identifiers only without copying sensitive details. R3 records contain identifiers and request categories only in the controlled area; M01 goes in the meeting area. Retention periods are unspecified; mark policy lookup pending, without inventing years or deleting files.

Three self-built table fields: transaction ledger = identifier / receipt / deadline / category / status / basis / referral / missing items; checking table = identifier / original value / difference / approval / response; filing handover = linked identifier / area / access holder / retention basis / outstanding tasks. First prevent R3 public disclosure and refer to I, then handle B01 and tell R2 verification is pending. M01's draft notice is due 11:00.
